title: Indigenous Environmental Network urges Congress to reject the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
content:
On Wednesday, in a shocking attack against Tribal sovereignty, Senate Democrats voted to move forward with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) (S. 5653), a bill steeped in environmental racism that would legally ensure the rapid buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure and AI data centers, while stripping away the federal-Tribal consultation process.

Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) are leading the effort, alongside far-right Republican colleagues Mike Lee (R-UT) and Shelley Capito (R-WV), to enact an aggressive attack on the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 Tribal consultation process. In addition to undermining Tribal consultation, the BAAJA erases protections under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act (CWA), and Endangered Species Act (ESA), paving the way to bring hyperscale data centers and natural gas projects online without critical guardrails for the land, water, and animals.

The Senate voted Wednesday 65-31 to invoke a cloture vote, which is a procedural vote that formally ends debate and allows the bill to move forward. Consideration of amendments is expected to begin Thursday, after which the bill will move into a final vote on passage before moving to the House. Despite the BAAJA being vastly opposed among climate justice groups, Tribal Nations, and Indigenous organizations, 14 Democrats voted to move forward with the bill; Chris Coons (DE), John Fetterman (PA), Ruben Gallego (AZ), Kirsten Gillibrand (NY), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (CO), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (NV), Brian Schatz (HI), Chuck Schumer (NY), Elissa Slotkin (MI), Mark Warner (VA), Raphael Warnock (GA), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI) all voted yes.

In perhaps the most egregious betrayal of all, the majority of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee–those Congress members charged with the highest responsibility to uphold the federal Treaty and Trust obligations–have continued to support stripping away Tribal consultation in the BAAJA. This includes Chairman Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Vice Chairman Brian Schatz (D-HI), as well as John Hoeven (R-ND), Steve Daines (R-MT), Jerry Moran (R-KS), and Alan Armstrong (R-OK).

Meanwhile, key Congressional environmental leaders and Tribal allies have strongly opposed the BAAJA and uplifted the concerns of Tribes and communities, including Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-AZ), and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI).

As an Indigenous organization representing grassroots Indigenous land protectors, the Indigenous Environmental Network stands with the hundreds of Tribal Nations, climate justice organizations, and community members strongly opposing this disaster bill. We encourage everyone to call your senators and representatives today to urge them to vote no on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to preserve our land and sovereignty for future generations.

The BAAJA is a violation of the federal Treaty and Trust obligations.

The BAAJA proposes sweeping changes to the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 Tribal consultation process that could effectively cut out Indigenous voices when determining whether a historically significant, sacred, or cultural site is worth protecting.

Congress and the federal government have a legally enforceable fiduciary obligation to protect Tribal Treaty rights, lands, assets, and resources, as contained in the framework of federal Indian law and legally binding Treaty-making. The Tribal consultation process is the basic function of this Treaty and Trust obligation, which has been codified since 1966 in the NHPA Section 106.

Under the BAAJA Sec. 2301, opportunities for Tribal input in permitting will be reduced and restricted in a way that reflects termination-era policy. Mandatory Section 106 Tribal consultation becomes optional, and agencies will no longer need to notify Tribal Nations before decisions are made that could impact sacred sites. The definitions of what agency actions require consultation and which cultural or historic properties qualify for protection is narrowed in such a way that cuts out a Tribe’s ability to define what is protected as sacred. Tribal Historic Preservation Officers (THPOs), often a Tribe’s greatest tool in preserving historic and cultural sites, will be under strict federal oversight with the risk of federal takeover. Along with State Historic Preservation Officers (SHPOs), THPOs could be subject to total takeover by the Secretary of the Interior if they fail to meet strict federal timelines and guidelines. The opportunity for Tribes to legally challenge decisions would be so restrictive that it would make it extremely difficult for a Tribe to legally enforce their rights. Claims would be subject to a “punitively short 150 day” limitation and strict criteria for who is even allowed to file suit.

Section 106 is the only codified standard for Tribal consultation in federal law, and the proposed changes are akin to a termination-era policy that seeks to diminish the Tribal-federal relationship and exclude Tribal voices rather than respecting the autonomy and self-governance of Tribes. Although the bill’s authors proposed some minor manager’s amendments to Sec. 2301 and 2302, the amendments do not meaningfully address the violations of Tribal consultation standards. Tribal Nations still strongly oppose the BAAJA in its entirety. The bill authors and Senate leaders will determine whether to allow an amendment to be heard, proposed by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA), to completely strike the NHPA section and preserve the Section 106 Tribal consultation process.

The BAAJA paves the way for more fossil fuels and AI data centers.

Far from being a “renewable energy bill” – this bill is designed to accelerate pipeline and natural gas projects, as well as data center expansion.

There is a reason the American Petroleum Institute, along with the CEOs of Enbridge, BP, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, ConocoPhillips, Devon Energy, EQT, Halliburton, Marathon Petroleum, Plains All American Pipeline, Shell, TC Energy, Williams, Woodside Energy, and Caturus, have fully endorsed and made passing the BAAJA a top legislative priority. The BAAJA creates vast categorical exemptions for gas pipeline expansions that will no longer be subject to environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Many of these gas expansions are requested to bring hyperscale data centers online.

The proposed changes to the Clean Water Act (CWA) would make it easier for pipelines to damage waterways. The BAAJA would significantly reduce the authority of states and Tribal Nations under CWA Section 401, especially their ability to enforce their own water protections. By increasing the burden of proof, shortening review periods, and favoring certain energy projects, the bill would lead to more water pollution, habitat destruction, and damage to waterways with less government oversight. States and Tribes would have less power to deny permits or require protections for waterways affected by pollution, runoff, erosion, and sedimentation. Section 1204 would limit the Army Corps of Engineers’ review of projects, making it harder to consider impacts such as habitat destruction, flooding, and harm to fish and wildlife. It would also automatically classify damage to less than two acres of water as having minimal environmental effects. For example, a pipeline could cross dozens of small streams, each affecting less than two acres, but collectively cause serious damage to an entire watershed.

The bill’s changes to federal environmental laws would also make it easier to approve data center projects on public lands with fewer delays and legal challenges. Under Executive Order 14318, the Trump administration has been considering at least 12 data center projects covering 17,600 acres of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) property in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming. Although the BLM approved the 88.5-acre Townsite Data Center in Nevada, construction is currently paused due to ongoing litigation. However, BAAJA’s proposed changes to NEPA would make challenges like these more difficult in the future. Other proposed developments include the 9,000-acre Project Beehive in Utah and the 3,200-acre Rhea Data Center in Idaho. These changes would also lead to an expansion of ICE detention centers on public lands.

The BAAJA rescinds bedrock environmental regulations.

This bill would restrict public participation and legal challenges under NEPA, the NHPA, and the CWA, while imposing a 150-day deadline for filing lawsuits. These restrictions make it considerably more difficult for affected communities, particularly Indigenous Peoples and communities of color, to challenge projects that threaten their land, resources, habitat, and health.

The BAAJA strips courts of the authority to halt an ongoing project, generally preventing them from vacating or enjoining project authorizations, even when a court determines that a permit was issued in violation of NEPA. Rather than allowing courts to invalidate an unlawful approval or halt a project through an injunction, the bill would require them to remand the decision to the responsible agency for reconsideration while the existing authorization remains in effect.

Additionally, the BAAJA would reduce the Fish and Wildlife Service’s ability to conduct inter-agency consultation, reducing the consultation period under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) from 90 days to 60 days, leaving less time to evaluate potential threats to endangered species. Certain projects could also be exempted from federal ESA reviews, with states assuming responsibility for the consultation process.

The BAAJA creates an open door for mills and mining waste disposal on public lands.

This bill would substantially expand the ability of mining companies to use public lands for industrial development by removing longstanding limits on the number and total acreage of mill sites used for processing, waste disposal, roads, pipelines, and other mining infrastructure. The BAAJA would allow companies to establish unlimited mill sites and potentially claim hundreds or thousands of acres of public land for mining waste disposal and storage.

Section 2215 would also undermine the court decision that blocked the Rosemont copper mine in Arizona from dumping toxic waste that threatened Hohokam burial grounds sacred to the Tohono O’odham Nation, Pascua Yaqui Tribe, and Hopi Tribe.

The BAAJA does not guarantee more renewable energy.

But it does guarantee more fossil fuels. Under Section 1401, the “project certainty” provision would make it difficult for future administrations to modify or revoke existing federal permits, even in response to new environmental information, health concerns, or policy changes. Section 1402 allows developers to sue federal agencies for “disparate treatment” – patterns of discriminatory permit delays or denials across specified energy industries, including renewable energy, fossil fuels, and mining. This is likely to result in locking in fossil fuel projects, as Trump has declared that his administration will not approve renewable projects, and companies will be permitted to default to the Trump administration’s favorable treatment towards fossil fuels.

In this heartless giveaway to fossil fuel companies, Senators Heinrich and Whitehouse are granting polluter corporations rights against “disparate treatment” that were originally reserved under the 1964 Civil Rights Act for protections against racial discrimination in the workplace, while simultaneously stripping Black and Indigenous communities and Tribal nations of their rights to challenge corporations threatening their health and livelihoods, resulting from cumulative impacts and disproportionate burdens.

Yet, even with generous predictions, the modeling only shows anywhere from a 0 to 4% reduction in emissions from the BAAJA–with some showing a risk that emissions would increase. It is simply not worth sacrificing Indigenous Peoples yet again, especially for such poor returns.

The “blue wave” will not save us if Democrats won’t stand up.

With the Democrats celebrating a sweeping win in the midterm elections and securing the majority in both houses of Congress, voters sent a clear message that Americans do not want more data centers or fossil fuels. It begs the question as to why those 14 Democrats would capitulate all of that power to Republican demands and big oil giveaways? Why would Democrats choose this moment to terminate the Tribal consultation process? Does the “blue wave” hit a brick wall when it comes to Indigenous sovereignty and Black and Brown communities? We need those 14 Senators to stand up for frontline communities and fulfill their Treaty and Trust obligations to Tribal Nations by having the courage to vote no on the BAAJA.

title: COP31
content:
Activists and civil society groups highlighted the impacts of the destructive greenwashed projects such as Pax Silica and intense militarization that continues to threaten livelihood, communities, and ecosystems.

COP31 should not be a space to further fuel wars but rather to demand accountability from the global military complex and its emissions. The solution is not more wars or military aggression but climate justice rooted in the realisation of people’s rights!
